title: A Voting Rule Needs a System Behind It
hook: Writing a new election rule is the easy part. Building the machinery that can execute it before the next election is where rules quietly turn into disenfranchisement.
key_points: Election administration is logistics: a rule only works if some agency can actually carry it out, at scale, on the calendar the law sets.
A March 2026 executive order directed the U.S. Postal Service to write rules requiring states to supply lists of mail-eligible voters and to use those lists to decide which ballots get delivered.
Per ProPublica, senior USPS officials warned internally that the rules could delay or block ballots for large numbers of eligible voters.

A whistleblower called the build secretive, rushed, chaotic and fundamentally flawed: development started in mid-June against a September 1 deadline, where comparable tracking systems typically take at least nine months.
Design choices compound the risk — the whistleblower said a single barcode failing to scan could cause an entire bulk batch of ballots to be rejected.
The general lesson: capacity, testing time, and failure modes are part of an election rule, not an afterthought to it.
content_html: Changing an election rule is a legal act; making it work is an engineering and logistics act. The gap between the two is where well-formed rules can quietly cost eligible people their votes.
extra_html: ProPublica's Jen Fifield reports that a March 2026 executive order directed the U.S. Postal Service to write regulations requiring states to hand over lists of mail-eligible voters, and requiring USPS to use those lists in deciding which ballots get sent. According to sources familiar with internal meetings, senior postal officials worried the rules "could delay or block ballots from reaching large swaths of eligible voters." An anonymous whistleblower, whose account NPR also reported through an interview with their lawyer and in Hansi Lo Wang's reporting, described the effort as "secretive, rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed": work began in mid-June against a September 1 deadline, while industry experts told ProPublica that comparable tracking systems normally take at least nine months to build. The failure modes matter as much as the schedule — the whistleblower said that if one barcode in a bulk mailing fails to scan, the whole batch is rejected, a concern election officials raised for jurisdictions that mail ballots by the million. The transferable point is not about any one order: whenever a rule changes how ballots move, the questions to ask are who executes it, on what timeline, and what happens when a step fails. (This card describes U.S. election administration specifically.)

related.title: Who Actually Sets the Rules for a Federal Election
related.hook: The Constitution hands the times, places and manner of congressional elections to state legislatures, with Congress able to override. The president is not on that list.

related.title: The Calendar as a Legal Strategy
related.hook: Courts avoid changing election rules close to voting day. That gives a litigant a strange incentive: argue the other side sued too early, and the clock does the rest.

related.title: Mail Ballot Grace Periods
related.hook: A ballot mailed on Election Day can still arrive days later. Should it count? States disagree — and in 2026 the Supreme Court sided with the states that say yes.

related.title: Why Vote Counts Shift After Election Night
related.hook: Watch a close race and the leader can flip in the days after polls close. The usual cause is boring — who votes by mail, and when those ballots get counted — not fraud.

flashcards.prompt: Why can a new election rule cause disenfranchisement even if nobody intends it to?
flashcards.back_html: Because the rule still has to be executed by real machinery. If the system behind it is built in a hurry and fails, eligible voters lose ballots regardless of the rule's stated purpose.

flashcards.prompt: What did the whistleblower say about how a barcode failure would affect a bulk mailing of ballots?

choices.text: One barcode failing to scan could cause the entire batch to be rejected
Only the single ballot with the bad barcode would be rejected
Barcodes are checked after delivery, so nothing would be rejected

flashcards.explanation_html: A batch-level failure mode turns one small defect into thousands of undelivered ballots — the kind of design detail that decides whether a rule is administrable.

flashcards.prompt: What timing problem did the whistleblower describe with the USPS verification system?

choices.text: Development began in mid-June against a September 1 deadline, where similar systems usually take at least nine months
The system was finished years early and then left unused
Congress required the system to launch only after the midterms

flashcards.explanation_html: Roughly ten weeks for something comparable builds normally taking nine months is the core capacity complaint in ProPublica's reporting.
